clue.text: Ceremony with which to pronounce a Spanish sentence

definitions.text: Ceremony with which to pronounce a Spanish sentence

parts.words: Ceremony with which to pronounce a Spanish sentence
parts.note: the Spanish Inquisition's public ritual at which its sentences on heretics were proclaimed; 'sentence' pretends to be grammar

explanation.surface: Someone hunts for the right formal occasion to utter a phrase in Spanish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sentence' reads as a string of Spanish words, but it is a judicial sentence: the Inquisition announced its verdicts at this 'act of faith'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Portuguese phrase means act of faith, the Inquisition's public ceremony of sentencing and punishing heretics.

clue.text: Archbishop gives brief reply to vulnerable tree

parts.note: ANS is the short form of answer, a reply
the elm, ravaged by Dutch elm disease, is a famously vulnerable tree

explanation.surface: A churchman sends a curt response to a sickly tree.
explanation.definitionFit: Saint Anselm was Archbishop of Canterbury under William II and Henry I.

clue.text: Satellite marine deity

explanation.surface: A heavenly body that is also a god of the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Neptune's largest moon bears the name, and in Greek myth he is the merman son of Poseidon who calms the waves with a conch.

clue.text: A good wife who "failed to look well to her linen"

definitions.text: A good wife who "failed to look well to her linen"

parts.words: A good wife who "failed to look well to her linen"
parts.note: echoes the virtuous wife of Proverbs who looks well to her household, here a faithful wife undone by a lost handkerchief

explanation.surface: A virtuous spouse is gently reproached for neglecting the laundry.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'linen' is the strawberry-spotted handkerchief in Othello whose loss Iago turns into false proof of adultery.
explanation.definitionFit: Othello's blameless wife is condemned because she mislaid the handkerchief he had given her.

clue.text: Book illustration is perfection, in a way

indicators.note: taken loosely, as letters put in another way or order, so they are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A fine picture in a book is said to be flawless after a fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a way' rearranges the letters of IS PERFECTION.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the decorative plate facing a book's title page.

clue.text: Writer of Christabel (locally celebrated)

indicators.note: the answer is taken out of the run of words that follows, so 'of' signals letters drawn from within

explanation.surface: A note on who wrote Coleridge's poem, which is famous in its home district.
explanation.walkthrough: Christabel was Coleridge's, not this writer's; the answer sits across the end of Christabel and the start of locally.
explanation.definitionFit: Hilaire Belloc was an Anglo-French author of essays, verse and the Cautionary Tales.

clue.text: Lamb lover in the deli — an enthusiastic carnivore

indicators.note: the letters lie inside the following words, straddling the dash

explanation.surface: Someone who loves lamb, found at the delicatessen, turns out to be a keen meat-eater.
explanation.walkthrough: Lamb is Charles Lamb, who wrote as Elia; the meat-eating surface hides him.
explanation.definitionFit: An admirer of Charles Lamb's Essays of Elia is called by an adjective formed from his pen name.

clue.text: Superlative second sequel to Jackie Collins opus (1965)

definitions.text: Superlative second sequel to Jackie Collins opus (1965)

parts.words: Superlative second sequel to Jackie Collins opus (1965)
parts.note: treats the novelist's title Lucky as an adjective: its comparative is a first follow-up and its superlative the second

explanation.surface: A note about a third book following a bestselling novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Jackie Collins wrote Lucky; the grammatical ladder of positive, comparative, superlative makes the superlative the 'second sequel'. The printed date is probably an OCR slip for 1985.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the superlative degree of the adjective naming the Jackie Collins novel, two steps along.

clue.text: Swann's metaphorical orchid

parts.note: in Proust, Swann and Odette use the name of this flower as their private code for making love

explanation.surface: A note on the flower that stood for something else in Proust.
explanation.definitionFit: In Swann's Way, arranging Odette's orchids becomes the lovers' euphemism for sex, so the flower's name is a metaphor.

clue.text: Ops, and pills combine to restore Fielding character

indicators.note: to restore here is to put the combined letters back into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Operations and medication together bring a character back to health.
explanation.walkthrough: 'restore' rearranges the letters of OPS and PILLS.
explanation.definitionFit: Mrs Slipslop is the amorous, word-mangling waiting-gentlewoman in Henry Fielding's Joseph Andrews.

clue.text: Melancholy as —- or a lugg'd bear" (King Henry the Fourth Part One)

parts.note: a quotation with a gap: Falstaff compares his gloom to that of a tomcat and a baited bear

explanation.surface: A line of Shakespeare with a word missing.
explanation.definitionFit: Falstaff says he is as melancholy as a tomcat, an old castrated male cat, or a bear led about by the ear.

clue.text: Suffering from "cirrhosis of the spirit", like Schulberg's Fitzgerald figure?

explanation.surface: A spiritually worn-out man resembles the hero of a novel about Fitzgerald.
explanation.definitionFit: Disillusion is a sickness of the spirit, and Budd Schulberg's novel about a Fitzgerald-like writer bears this word as its title.

clue.text: African money for Italian director ()

explanation.surface: Cash from Africa paid to a film-maker from Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: The '()' after the clue is a printing remnant and plays no part.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the currency of Sierra Leone, and Sergio Leone directed spaghetti westerns such as The Good, the Bad and the Ugly.

clue.text: Third-year celebration — find it in Arlen, perhaps

indicators.note: signals that the letters of the words given may be arranged some other way

explanation.surface: A celebration in the third year can be found in the work of Arlen, maybe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges the letters of IT IN ARLEN; 'find' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Something happening every third year, such as a festival, is described by this word.

clue.text: He brought Bernstein along in a Tanglewood tale

definitions.text: He brought Bernstein along in a Tanglewood tale

parts.words: He brought Bernstein along in a Tanglewood tale
parts.note: the conductor who taught and championed the young Leonard Bernstein at the Tanglewood summer school; Tanglewood Tales is also a Hawthorne title

explanation.surface: A man nurtures a young talent in a story set in Massachusetts.
explanation.walkthrough: Tanglewood is the Boston Symphony's summer home, where Serge Koussevitzky (this spelling) mentored Bernstein; the phrase also nods to Hawthorne's Tanglewood Tales.
explanation.definitionFit: The Russian-born conductor of the Boston Symphony founded the Tanglewood school and was Bernstein's mentor.

clue.text: Balkan state attracting early Italian visitors

definitions.text: Balkan state attracting early Italian visitors

parts.words: Balkan state attracting early Italian visitors
parts.note: a land on the eastern Adriatic that drew Romans, the earliest Italian visitors, who made it a province

explanation.surface: A tourism note about a Balkan country popular with Italians long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'early Italian visitors' were Roman conquerors, who gave the region this Latin name as a province.
explanation.definitionFit: It was the Roman province covering the western Balkans along the Adriatic coast.

clue.text: " —— does not mean that you forget" (Steve Biko)

parts.words: " —— does not mean that you forget" (Steve Biko)
parts.note: a quotation with a gap from the South African anti-apartheid activist

explanation.surface: A line from Steve Biko with a word missing.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is a present participle meaning adjusting to new circumstances, which Biko says need not mean forgetting.

clue.text: Cythera was a banal one, Baudelaire thought

parts.words: Cythera was a banal one, Baudelaire thought
parts.note: in Un voyage à Cythère Baudelaire calls Venus's island a commonplace golden land of every old bachelor's dreams

explanation.surface: A French poet dismisses a Greek island of love as unoriginal.
explanation.definitionFit: Baudelaire calls Cythera the banal version of the fabled city of gold that every old bachelor dreams of.

clue.text: Name of the little Italian woman composer

definitions.text: Name of the little Italian woman composer

parts.words: Name of the little Italian woman composer
parts.note: read as Italian, the composer's surname translates as of the little one, feminine

explanation.surface: A request for the name of a short female composer from Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is a translation: Italian 'dalla piccola' means 'of the little (woman)', and Luigi Dallapiccola was a twentieth-century Italian composer.
explanation.definitionFit: Luigi Dallapiccola was an Italian twelve-tone composer, and his surname literally means of the little girl.

clue.text: Spenserian handle for essayist, say

parts.note: Richard Steele co-founded The Spectator and The Tatler with Addison

explanation.surface: A nickname from Spenser for a writer of essays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'handle' looks like a nickname but is the handle of a tool; Spenser spells it this way.
explanation.definitionFit: In Spenser's archaic spelling the word means the handle or shaft of an implement.

clue.text: It was finished by Greene

parts.note: points to the Graham Greene novel whose title declares that something is over

explanation.surface: A remark that Graham Greene completed some work.
explanation.walkthrough: Graham Greene's novel The End of the Affair puts an end to this word.
explanation.definitionFit: Greene titled his novel The End of the Affair, so a love affair is what he ended.

clue.text: "Let the Egyptians and the us go a ducking" (Antony and Cleopatra)

parts.words: "Let the Egyptians and the us go a ducking" (Antony and Cleopatra)
parts.note: a quotation with a gap: Enobarbus says the eastern sea peoples should fight on water, not the Romans

explanation.surface: A line of Shakespeare with letters missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed line is damaged: Shakespeare writes 'the Phoenicians', so the answer fills the gap and the surviving fragment supplies the ending.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient seafaring land of Tyre and Sidon on the Levant coast gives the people Enobarbus mentions.

clue.text: A mother of twelve, she was petrified ()

definitions.text: A mother of twelve, she was petrified

parts.words: A mother of twelve, she was petrified
parts.note: the Theban queen who boasted of her many children, saw them killed and was turned to stone

explanation.surface: A mother with a large family was terrified.
explanation.walkthrough: 'petrified' reads as frightened, but she was literally turned to stone weeping. The '()' after the clue is a printing remnant.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth this queen's children were slain by Apollo and Artemis and she became a weeping rock.

clue.text: French fantasist from cabaret, if you please!

indicators.note: the letters are drawn from within the words that follow

explanation.surface: A French dreamer comes out of a nightclub, if you please.
explanation.definitionFit: Restif (or Rétif) de la Bretonne was an eighteenth-century French novelist of erotic and utopian fantasies.

clue.text: Chekhov anti-hero produces a number between four and five

clue.text: Staccato sort of thrust

clue.text: Stevenson character obtained from war media
